query: Which decision rules will determine REML versus Bayesian estimation and what priors will we use for hierarchical Bayesian power analyses?

response.query: Which decision rules will determine REML versus Bayesian estimation and what priors will we use for hierarchical Bayesian power analyses?
response.answer: REML is preferred for unbiased parameter estimation in mixed models; Bayesian estimation uses diffuse priors for small samples. For hierarchical Bayesian power analyses, use weakly informative priors.

results.title: A comparison of Bayesian and likelihood-based methods for fitting ...
results.content: Keywords: Adaptive MCMC, bias, calibration, diﬀuse priors, hierarchical model-ing, hybrid Metropolis-Gibbs sampling, intraclass correlation, IGLS, interval cover-age, MQL, mixed models, PQL, RIGLS, random-eﬀects logistic regression, REML, variance-components models ∗Division of Statistics, School of Mathematical Sciences, University of Nottingham, UK †Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics, University of California, Santa Cruz, CA, c ⃝2006 International Society for Bayesian Analysis ba0003 474 Bayesian and likelihood-based methods in multilevel modeling 1 Introduction Multilevel models, for data possessing a nested hierarchy and—more generally—for the expression of uncertainty at several levels of aggregation, have gained dramati-cally in scope of application in the past 15 years, in ﬁelds as diverse as education and health policy (e.g., Goldstein et al. • In two-level VC models with a wide variety of sample sizes and true parameter values, – Both likelihood-based (ML and REML) and Bayesian (diﬀuse-prior) methods can be made to yield approximately unbiased point estimates, in the likeli-hood case by using REML rather than ML estimates, and in the Bayesian case by choosing one of several combinations of diﬀuse priors and posterior point summaries (speciﬁcally, for random-eﬀects variances: posterior medi-ans for Γ−1(ϵ, ϵ) priors and posterior modes for U(0, 1 ϵ ) priors, in both cases for small ϵ; these combinations produce approximate unbiasedness in all but the smallest designs (i.e., those with fewer than about a dozen cluster units in the hierarchy)). Likelihood-based intervals of the kind we have studied here underperform in that situation for a fundamental reason that would be harder to remedy: the insistence on maximization (rather than integration) over the parameters of a highly-skewed likelihood surface with its marginal maximum at σ2 u = 0 leads to zero point es-timates in small samples with some frequency when the true value is well away from 0; • The usual quasi-likelihood computer output in RELR models may not be trust-worthy either for point estimation or uncertainty assessment, in the latter case because the estimated asymptotic standard errors can be systematically too small when the mean numbers of level–k units per level–(k+1) unit (and/or the number of level–M units in an M–level model) are small for k ≥1; and • There is an expectation, expressed formally in the Bernstein-von Mises theo-rem (e.g., Freedman (1999); also see Samaniego and Reneau (1994) and Severini (1994)), that likelihood and diﬀuse-prior Bayesian results will be close in large sam-ples, and this will typically occur when parametric models with a modest number of parameters are ﬁt to data not possessing a hierarchical structure.

results.title: Use of Bayesian hierarchical model - Cross Validated
results.content: # Use of Bayesian hierarchical model. What is the purpose of Bayesian hierarchical model? My doubts are about the application of such models, and about their use as substitute of non-informative priors. > *Hierarchical models* mediate two needs: the need to incorporate in the analysis "a priori" opinions about the coefficients of the model and the use of non-informative priors which, if not conjugated, involve big computational problems. $\begingroup$ There is no opposition between hierarchical models and non-informative priors. My professor's notes present hierarchical models as an alternative to the use of non-informative priors in one stage. $\begingroup$ I suppose what your professor may be trying to say is that instead of 1) doing something with prior knowledge to somehow formulate some prior for a new analysis, he instead 2) embeds all information into a single hierarchical model that implicitly induces a prior. To the best of my knowledge, there is no opposition between Bayesian models (BM) and hierarchical Bayesian models (HBM) (see e.g. Relation between Bayesian analysis and Bayesian hierarchical analysis?) and the fact is that, analytically, HBMs are BMs. Hierarchical models simply allow you to design a convoled prior structures that is more likely to represents e.g. interactions between variables of your model and thus to provide more suited inference. I added the point which makes me doubtful about the use of hierarchical prior information and non-informative prior distributions. * when should I use a hierarchical model? ### When should I use a hierarchical model? In contast, if the groups have very different means, then $\sigma^2$ will be large and the resulting inference for the individual $\theta\_j$ will be almost the same as you didn't have the hierarchical model at all. Thus you didn't have to choose whether to use a model with a common mean for all groups or a completely independent mean for all groups, the hierarchical model allowed the data to tell you where you fell along that continuum. Once you have decided to use a hierarchical model for your data, there is still the question of how you will estimate parameters and account for their uncertainty.

results.title: Demystifying Priors in Bayesian Modeling
results.content: In this article, we will demystify priors in Bayesian modeling by exploring theoretical underpinnings and practical implementations, and discussing diagnostic checks necessary for ensuring robust inference. Bayesian updating through this theorem allows us to blend prior knowledge with observed evidence, providing a probabilistic framework for parameter estimation that adapts as new data arrives 1. Priors play a vital role in Bayesian modeling by influencing the posterior estimates, particularly in cases of limited data. This diagram illustrates the dual paths of specifying priors and highlights that while the data collection and Bayesian update processes are common, the nature of the prior can shape the resultant posterior in significantly different ways. data { int N; vector[N] x; vector[N] y; } parameters { real alpha; real beta; real sigma; } model { // Priors alpha ~ normal(0, 10); beta ~ normal(0, 10); sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5); // Likelihood y ~ normal(alpha + beta * x, sigma); } #### PyMC Example Using PyMC, the same linear regression model can be implemented as follows: ```python import pymc as pm import numpy as np N = 100 x = np.linspace(0, 10, N) y = 2.5 + 1.5 * x + (0, 1, N) with pm.Model() as model: # Priors alpha = pm.Normal("alpha", mu=0, sigma=10) beta = pm.Normal("beta", mu=0, sigma=10) sigma = pm.HalfCauchy("sigma", beta=5) # Likelihood mu = alpha + beta * x y_obs = pm.Normal("y_obs", mu=mu, sigma=sigma, observed=y) # MCMC sampling trace = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000) Both tools facilitate clear prior block definitions and allow for efficient posterior sampling using MCMC methods 4 5. Many modern Bayesian software packages provide diagnostic functions that verify prior predictive distributions, ensuring that the priors lead to reasonable predictions even before data are fit. With a solid understanding of priors and diagnostic tools, we now explore advanced applications in Bayesian modeling. By grounding our approach in well-established Bayesian foundations, leveraging contemporary software implementations, and rigorously applying diagnostic checks, we can build models that reliably integrate both prior knowledge and observed data. From introductory Bayes’ theorem to advanced applications like hierarchical modeling and empirical Bayes methods, this article has illustrated how a thoughtful choice and assessment of priors underpin sound Bayesian inference.

results.title: Moving beyond noninformative priors: why and how to choose weakly informative priors in Bayesian analyses
results.content: Specifically, Bayesian estimated parameters and inferences based on noninformative priors will be identical to frequentist analyses with standard methods (e.g. the lm or glm functions in R, Gelman et al. Thus, ecologists should consider adopting a normal-gamma or hierarchical weakly informative prior as a default prior for regressions; such priors conservatively estimate parameters and mitigate type M errors with low-powered data but have little impact on posterior inference with high-powered data. Treatment estimates for high-powered data, resulting from either low noise (σ*y* = 2) or larger sample sizes (N = 30) exhibited less regularization with weakly informative priors (Fig. 7). I recommend that ecologists use the Cauchy priors when modeling correlated random effects for four reasons: 1) the decomposed components are easily interpretable, τ contains variances and Ω is the correlation matrix, 2) the Cauchy alone yielded proper posteriors across all sample sizes, 3) priors can be easily be strengthened or weakened via Cauchy and LKJ distributions, or by replacing Cauchy(0,1) with , and 4) Cauchy posteriors converged towards the noninformative scaled InvWish prior at high sample sizes. Regularization can potentially mitigate or eliminate common errors associated with frequentist or noninformative Bayesian analyses, and weakly informative priors are simple to implement in any standard Bayesian model (Supplementary material Appendix 1–7). Even the modest regularization provided by weakly informative priors with low statistical power can reduce type I errors (Fig. 5) and improve out-of-sample prediction for regression models (McElreath 2015). In ANOVA models, shrinkage provided by regularization priors can eliminate the need for post-hoc corrections for multiple comparisons; pairwise contrasts of weakly informed posteriors often have lower error rates than Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons among noninformed posteriors (Gelman et al. results.content: # What is the relationship between graphical models and hierarchical Bayesian models? My impression is that in the Machine Learning literature you'll find allusions to hierarchical Bayesian modeling, but in the Statistics literature you'll seldom find allusions to PGMs. Hopefully you guys will be able to allay my confusion. 1. Since Hierarchical Bayesian models are also DAGs, can you use the message passing algorithms of PGMs (junction tree etc.) in this context? (This sounds like you make a kind of clustering model every time you abstract away a node in the hierarchy with a parent). ## 3 Answers 3. Graphical models are graphs which encode independencies between the random variables in the model. A graphical model with the assumptions on random variables can give us the joint distribution given the parameters. We may or may not know the parameters of the graphical models. By being more bayesian I mean that I want to model the uncertainty in the estimation of the table and I would like to model distribution over tables, i.e. distribution over discrete distribution in this case. By similar argument we want to model the uncertainty in the hyperparameters and set priors over them. answered Jan 14, 2014 at 21:32. My understanding is that a hierarchical model can be represented by a DAG. Hence all our knowledge about probabilistic graphical models applies. One difference (which is not really a difference) is that in hierarchical models, usually hyperpriors are included. Or at least hyperpriors are discussed in the context of hierarchical models more often.
